newsitem.title: BRAZIL: New owners not seen splitting up Brazil CVRD.
newsitem.headline: New owners not seen splitting up Brazil CVRD.

text.p: The new controlling shareholders of Brazilian mining giant CVRD are unlikely to split up the privatized company or spin off its different operations, analysts said.
Valepar, an international consortium led by Brazil's largest steelmaker CSN, took a 41.73 percent voting stake in CVRD for $3.15 billion at the company's privatization auction Tuesday.

"Valepar would benefit from keeping CVRD in one piece," said Raphael Biderman, analyst at investment bank Robert Fleming in Sao Paulo. "When you split some parts of CVRD you destroy value, especially if you split mining and transportation."
CVRD is the world's largest iron ore producer and exporter, but also mines gold, bauxite, copper and other metals, produces pulp and paper and runs its own railways, ports and shipping companies.

Biderman said it would not make sense for Valepar to sell any of CVRD's businesses, except perhaps its pulp and paper operations, because the various members of the consortium all had vested interests in different aspects of CVRD.

He said CSN had an interest in keeping CVRD's aluminium operations, while the pension funds had an interest in copper production and CVRD's gold mining was the most promising sector with the best growth prospects.

Apart from CSN, Valepar includes four local pension funds, NationsBank Corp and Brazil's Opportunity Asset Management with its offshore investment fund for foreign, mainly U.S., investors like Citicorp and George Soros.

Banco Graphus Director Sergio Zendron said CVRD's various lines of business would probably be reorganized into different subsidiaries whose performance would be measured by international industry standards in the different sectors and improve as a result.
CSN Chairman Benjamin Steinbruch confirmed shortly after the privatization auction that Valepar in fact had no plans to divide up the company and sell it off in bits and pieces.
"We don't plan to split up or to dismember the company," he said. "CVRD gains value if it stays in one piece."
He said Valepar would study CVRD in depth over a six-month period after which any necessary changes would be introduced "slowly" and "progressively". No job cuts were planned, he added.
Analysts said privatization's biggest effect on the company would be an improvement in efficiency, greater flexibility in decision-making and enhanced investment capabilities.

"CVRD will become more efficient because a lot of the bureaucracy involved in being a state company is being eliminated as a result of privatization," said Rodrigo Marques, analyst at investment bank Bozano Simonsen.
Marques said Valepar was unlikely to carry out large job cuts, but Biderman said there was room to cut costs by getting rid of up to 15 percent of CVRD's current workforce of more than 15,400.

Biderman said the fact that none of the members of Valepar were actual clients of CVRD's core iron ore business meant that they would focus on turning CVRD into a profit center by negotiating prices more aggressively and increasing production.

He estimated that CVRD's profit would grow around 36 percent over the next three years and that investment levels would rise by 45 to 50 percent over the same time period. CVRD's plans investment this year is of $600 million.
